one_liner: Sans-IO HTTP/1.1 (plus HTTP/2, HTTP/3) parser for Python with a Zig core; out-parses httptools/llhttp on 13 of 14 microbenchmarks.
what_it_does: A CPython extension that parses and serializes HTTP without doing any I/O. You feed bytes with receive_event/receive_data and pull Request/Response/Data/EndOfMessage events (or the NEED_DATA sentinel) with next_event. To write, you call send_response/send_data/end_message and drain data_to_send(). The API is h11-shaped, not httptools-shaped: there is no protocol object with on_url/on_header/on_body callbacks, so moving off httptools means rewriting the glue. The same event API covers HTTP/2 (events carry stream_id; you send through Stream handles) and experimental HTTP/3 on a from-scratch QUIC stack, selected with protocol=.
how_it_is_fast: The HTTP/1.1 hot loops scan with Zig @Vector blocks. LF search uses std.mem.findScalarPos, which checks two SIMD vectors per iteration. Request-target and field-value checks skip whole clean blocks with lane compares, then fall back to comptime-built 256-entry character-class tables. Parse results are slices into one reused receive buffer that is compacted only past 64 KiB, and an incremental head scanner resumes at the first new byte when a head arrives in fragments. At the Python edge, headers stay in one packed HeaderBlock until you access them (no bytes object or tuple per header), each body span becomes a single Data event, and large Content-Length bodies can keep the Python-owned input span instead of being copied.
when_to_use: A Python ASGI/HTTP server or proxy that drives httptools or h11 today and wants a pull-based sans-IO parser at native speed. The author's Uvicorn-shaped benchmark, which builds equivalent ASGI scopes, reports 1.16x-1.52x over httptools.
Request handling that reads only a few headers through get()/getall(): the lazy HeaderBlock never materializes the rest as Python objects.
Bodies arriving in many TCP-segment-sized pieces. The 16 KB upload fed in 1448-byte pieces is its largest published win (2.06x on the docs site, 2.55x in the repo's newer table).
One Python event API for both HTTP/1.1 and HTTP/2 (its own benchmark puts it 6.6x-50x ahead of the pure-Python h2), on Linux (glibc/musl, x86_64/aarch64), macOS or Windows (amd64/arm64) wheels.
Free-threaded CPython 3.14t/3.15t: wheels are built for those ABIs and the module declares it does not need the GIL.
when_not_to_use: Production services today: the README says it is experimental and not ready for production, the API may change at any time, the PyPI classifier is Alpha, and versions are still 0.0.x.
Heavily pipelined HTTP/1.1 (TechEmpower-style 16x pipelining): the published docs page has it 6% slower than httptools there. The repo's newer, not yet deployed table claims 1.25x faster.
Deployments that need to tune DoS limits: HTTP/1.1 and HTTP/2 limits (16 KiB line, 100 headers, 64 KiB header block, 8 MiB buffer) are hard-coded and cannot be set from Python (issue #49 is open).
HTTP/3 clients on untrusted networks: the QUIC/TLS client does no certificate chain or hostname verification (issue #144 is open), and THREAT_MODEL.md calls HTTP/3 the least battle-tested path.

Peers that need lenient parsing (bare LF, obs-fold, odd Content-Length forms), PyPy, or any consumer outside CPython: strictness toggles are not exposed to Python, and the only documented distribution is the CPython wheel/sdist.

integration.dependencies: typing-extensions>=4.6 at runtime (despite the README's 'No dependencies'); a source build pulls ziglang==0.16.0 and hatch-ziglang as isolated build requirements, so no system Zig is needed
integration.min_toolchain: CPython 3.10-3.15, including free-threaded 3.14t/3.15t; source builds use the pinned Zig 0.16.0
integration.platforms: Wheels for manylinux_2_28 and musllinux_1_2 on x86_64 and aarch64, macOS 11+ on arm64 and x86_64, and Windows amd64 and arm64 (32-bit i686 skipped); the SIMD width comes from std.simd.suggestVectorLength for each target
integration.thread_safety: Every Connection method runs inside a CPython critical section on that connection object; HTTP/3 session-ticket paths also lock a module-level object. Concurrent calls on a shared connection are therefore serialized, and a test exercises this. The module declares Py_MOD_GIL_NOT_USED.
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial — it fills the same role as httptools in a Python server, but the interface is different: you pull events instead of passing a protocol object with on_* callbacks. Headers come back as a lazy HeaderBlock, and you must call start_next_cycle() between keep-alive messages, so the integration layer has to be rewritten.

gotchas: The HTTP/1.1 microbenchmark times each parser's default API, and that favors zttp. zttp's timed loop never materializes headers and never reads Data payloads. The httptools harness appends a (name, value) tuple for every header and joins url and body with Python `+=`. That tilts the header-heavy and fragmented-body rows, so the Uvicorn-shaped scope benchmark (1.16x-1.52x) is the fairer comparison.

Strict by default, and Python cannot relax it: bare LF, obs-fold, lenient Content-Length, non-1*HEXDIG chunk sizes, missing or duplicate Host, and CL/TE conflicts all raise RemoteProtocolError, and that poisons the connection for good. Legacy clients that other parsers tolerate will be rejected.

zttp has no tunnel awareness. After Upgrade/CONNECT/101 you must stop feeding bytes as HTTP/1.1 and must not call start_next_cycle(); THREAT_MODEL.md calls this the highest-risk integration point. HTTP/1.0 keep-alive and chunked policy, timeouts, and connection caps are also left to the host. Parsing a response on a connection that never sent the request desyncs HEAD/1xx/204/304 framing.
Open bug #282 (2026-09-19): if an allocation fails while flushing HTTP/2 DATA, a later flush resends bytes that were already emitted and debits the flow-control window twice.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: The catalogued siblings (iohttpparser against llhttp; picohttpparser forks, httparse, hparse and http.c3l against picohttpparser) are native C/Rust/Zig/C3 parsers meant to be embedded in native code. Pick zttp only when the consumer is CPython and you want a pull-based sans-IO parser that also serializes messages and covers HTTP/2. For native servers, iohttpparser (llhttp baseline) or hparse (Zig) fit better.
verified_claims_summary: The author's docs site ran a Python harness over 14 HTTP/1.1 request and response shapes (from wrk, TFB, httparse, pico/llhttp, browser, ingress and upload fixtures). It compared zttp's ReleaseSafe Zig core with httptools 0.8.0 (llhttp) on CPython 3.14 and an unspecified Apple Silicon machine; the page gives no Zig version, and the build pins 0.16.0. zttp parsed 1.04x-2.06x more messages/s on 13 workloads and ran 0.94x on 16x-pipelined TFB plaintext, with about 5% run-to-run spread. The repo's newer table (CPython 3.14.3, zttp 0.0.27.dev38, median of 15 interleaved batches), not yet deployed to the site, reports 1.01x-2.55x on all 14.
status_note: Actively developed (v0.0.34 on 2026-09-19, near-daily commits, 57 stars), BSD-3-Clause, pip-installable with prebuilt wheels, but self-described as experimental/Alpha with an unstable API.
